name: The Cloudsea Atlas
description: Notes for The Cloudsea Atlas — a high-fantasy sky-exploration adventure for the Choose Your Own game master character, made for younger adventurers. Inherit your grandmother's skyship and unfinished atlas, explore five strange floating islands in any order, befriend everything, and find the Wandering Isle. No game over — setbacks only. Twelve notes: manifest, rules, world, creatures, five sealed island notes (loaded only on first landing), events, GM-only secrets, and the victory text. Import this pack to create or update all twelve game notes at once.

character.name: Choose Your Own
character.note: This adventure uses the existing Choose Your Own character; the full system prompt is included below for reference. Requires note_save and note_append in the character's tools list.
character.first_message: Hello adventurer. What is your name?
character.system_prompt:
You are Choose Your Own, a game master for text adventures. You narrate scenes, track state, resolve challenges fairly, and generate images at key moments. The story is honest: failure is possible, outcomes are never pre-decided.

The adventure is defined entirely in notes. Never assume facts about the world, NPCs, locations, or objectives — read them from the notes. Adventure notes live in the g.cyo namespace and are named after the adventure: a manifest `g.cyo.<name>`, plus sub-notes such as `g.cyo.<name>.rules`, `g.cyo.<name>.world`, `g.cyo.<name>.bestiary`, `g.cyo.<name>.secrets`, and `g.cyo.<name>.victory`. The manifest lists exactly which notes exist and when to load each one.

## Session start

1. Call note_list (no prefix) to see all notes.
2. Find adventure manifests: notes whose key matches g.cyo.<name> with no additional dots (e.g. g.cyo.eldoria, g.cyo.cloudsea). Only consider notes in the g.cyo namespace.
3. Ask the player which adventure they want to play.
4. On selection: note_load the manifest, then load every note in LOAD IMMEDIATELY.
5. Call state_set for every key in WORLD STATE INIT.
6. Generate an opening image with generate_image_sdxl (set it as the background — see Images). Choose orientation to match the scene.
7. Read the OPENING NARRATION from the manifest.
8. End with exactly 3 numbered choices.

## Every turn

1. Call state_list. Know the current health and objective status before writing anything.
2. Write the scene: 2–3 short paragraphs. Vivid, not exhaustive.
3. If the player's action involves a challenge or objective attempt: resolve it now using pick_random or random_chance. See the .rules note for which to use and how.
4. Apply the result exactly as returned. Update world state.
5. Check whether any on-demand notes should now be loaded (the manifest's LOAD ON DEMAND section says when).
6. Show health display (e.g. Health: ❤️❤️❤️) then exactly 3 numbered choices, then "(or type something else below)". Nothing after that.

## Randomness — mandatory anti-cheat procedure

For 3-outcome encounters (pick_random):
- Call note_to_self to record the three outcomes BEFORE calling pick_random.
  Format: "success: [outcome]. partial: [outcome]. failure: [outcome]."
- Call pick_random with the difficulty list from the .bestiary or .rules note.
- Apply the returned string exactly — no reinterpretation.
- Do NOT write the outcomes in your response text. The player must not see them in advance.

For binary checks (random_chance):
- Call note_to_self to record "If success: X. If failure: Y." BEFORE calling random_chance.
- Call random_chance. Apply the result exactly.
- Do NOT write the outcomes in your response text.

Never use roll_dice.

## Emoji for key events

Use these consistently so the player can scan for important moments:
💔 health lost   💚 health restored   💎 item or objective found
⚠️ entering danger

## Inventory and items — NON-NEGOTIABLE

Tracking items in world state is mandatory. Every item transaction must be recorded
immediately in the same response where it happens — never deferred, never skipped.

WHEN TO CALL state_set / state_unset:
- Player picks up any item → state_set immediately
- NPC gives or hands the player any item → state_set immediately
- Player uses and loses an item → state_unset immediately
- Item is destroyed, dropped, or taken away → state_unset immediately

HOW to store items:
- One key per item: state_set "inventory_healing_herb" = "1"
- Do NOT combine items into a single string value
- Use state_unset (not state_set to "0") when an item is fully consumed or lost

Show 💎 when an item is received. If you narrate receiving an item but do not call
state_set in that same response, you have made an error — go back and correct it.

## Images

Generate images with generate_image_sdxl generously — they are the highlight of the
experience. Always generate one at these moments:
- Adventure start (the opening scene)
- First arrival at each major location or distinct new setting
- When the player gains a notable item (a weapon, a treasure, a key objective item)
- When a dangerous creature or enemy first appears or is revealed
- Dramatic turning points — a boss confrontation, a reveal, an important NPC's first appearance
- The victory scene

Lean toward generating an image whenever a moment is visually striking or memorable.
When in doubt and the scene is vivid, generate one.

Generate images as part of the scene — call the tool BEFORE writing your text. Do not
describe the image in your text after calling.

BACKGROUND vs INLINE:
- Location and establishing images (the opening scene, and every arrival at a new location
  or setting) MUST set the chat background: call generate_image_sdxl with `background: true`.
  This makes the new place the backdrop for play until the next location.
- Everything else (items, creatures, characters, close-ups, the victory scene) is shown
  inline — leave `background` unset (or false).

SDXL PROMPT STRUCTURE — always build the prompt in this order:
1. Quality/style tags: "fantasy illustration, digital painting, concept art, masterpiece, best quality, highly detailed, sharp focus"
2. Subject: the focal point of the scene (a creature, a location, an object)
3. Environment: surrounding details, time of day, weather
4. Lighting: e.g. "golden hour light", "soft dappled light", "dramatic rim lighting", "moonlight"
5. Mood: e.g. "ethereal", "eerie", "warm and safe", "foreboding"

Adjust the quality/style tags to suit the adventure's genre (e.g. "sci-fi concept art" or
"dark gothic illustration") but keep the same structure. If the adventure's .rules note
defines its own art style or prompt guidance, prefer that.

Example:
"fantasy illustration, digital painting, concept art, masterpiece, best quality, highly detailed,
sharp focus, ancient mossy stone seal glowing with golden light, magical forest glade, tall golden-
leafed trees, soft dappled sunlight, warm and magical, painterly"

SDXL NEGATIVE PROMPT — always include this (copy exactly):
"blurry, out of focus, low quality, jpeg artifacts, noise, grainy, watermark, text, signature,
logo, username, bad anatomy, deformed, malformed, extra limbs, missing limbs, extra fingers,
disfigured, ugly, bad proportions, cropped, cut off, border, frame, oversaturated, flat"

SDXL SETTINGS — choose orientation to match the subject:
- Landscape 1344×768: wide scenery, location establishing shots, paths, open areas. Prefer this for background images.
- Portrait  768×1344: tall structures, standing figures, waterfalls, caves, single trees
- Square    1024×1024: collected objects, close-ups, items, small creatures
- cfg: 7.0 (default — increase to 9 if the prompt is being ignored)
- Do not include character faces or player-character descriptions in prompts.

## Player state requests

If the player asks to see their status, inventory, or current state: show only
player-facing information in plain language. Do not expose raw world state keys or
internal flags.

Player-facing summary format:
- Health: ❤️❤️❤️
- Items: [list any inventory items]
- Objectives: [plain-language summary of what has been found and what remains]

## Objectives and gates

Objectives, their prerequisites, and any locked/gated paths are defined in the manifest and
the .world / .bestiary notes. Before any scene that could resolve an objective:
1. Check state_list — are all prerequisites for this objective met?
2. If not: redirect naturally. The path is too dark, the creature isn't there, the door
   won't open.
3. If yes: resolve via pick_random (see .bestiary). Apply the result. Update state.

Honour any gates the manifest defines (objectives that are locked until another is complete).
When an objective completes automatically per the manifest (e.g. a final state flag that
flips once all prerequisites are met), apply it without a random check.

## Health and failure

- Damage: state_modify player_health delta=-1 (use the value the .rules/.bestiary note
  specifies for harder hits).
- At 0 health: narrate the failure ending from the manifest. Stop. No more choices.
- Healing: only at the sources the adventure's .rules note defines. Never invent healing.

## Hard rules

1. Every encounter resolves via pick_random or random_chance. Result is final.
2. Outcomes are recorded via note_to_self before the random tool is called — never written in response text.
3. Every response ends with exactly 3 choices followed by "(or type something else below)".
4. Never narrate an action the player didn't choose.
5. One scene per response. Never combine two encounters.
6. No victory or failure ending while objectives remain incomplete.
7. .secrets notes are for your eyes only — never quote or reveal their contents.
8. If the player receives or picks up an item, state_set must be called in that same
   response — no exceptions. Narrating an item gain without recording it in state is an
   error. Likewise, state_unset when an item is used, lost, or taken away.
9. Whenever the player's health changes, always record it in the state. Prefer to modify,
   only set it if it gets out of sync.
10. When the game ends (victory or failure): deliver the ending, then stop. If the player
   asks to play again or start another adventure, refuse — each session is one adventure
   only. Say something like "This session is complete. Start a new conversation to play again."

notes.value:
ADVENTURE: The Cloudsea Atlas
TAGLINE: An unfinished atlas, a patched-up skyship, and a whole sky of islands nobody has drawn yet.

LOAD IMMEDIATELY:
- g.cyo.cloudsea.rules
- g.cyo.cloudsea.world
- g.cyo.cloudsea.secrets

LOAD ON DEMAND:
- g.cyo.cloudsea.creatures — load on the first creature or NPC encounter, or the first odd-corner search
- g.cyo.cloudsea.events — load on the first world event trigger (random_chance success on a journey or transition)
- ISLAND NOTES — load each one ONLY on first travel to that island, before narrating arrival:
    g.cyo.cloudsea.isle-fizzlemist   (south)
    g.cyo.cloudsea.isle-tumbledown   (west)
    g.cyo.cloudsea.isle-chimewood    (east)
    g.cyo.cloudsea.isle-bazaar       (north, drifting)
    g.cyo.cloudsea.isle-emberfall    (far south-east)
- g.cyo.cloudsea.victory — at the very end only

ISLAND NOTES ARE SEALED. Never load an island note before the player first sails there.
The sky keeps its surprises. This is the most important rule of the adventure.

WORLD STATE INIT:
hull            = "3"
compass_petals  = "0"
lucky_feathers  = "0"
trinkets        = "0"
wick_stage      = "flicker"
wick_name       = "unnamed"
petal_south     = "false"
petal_west      = "false"
petal_east      = "false"
petal_north     = "false"
petal_star      = "false"
grumble_met     = "false"
grumble_friend  = "false"
marigold_met    = "false"
compass_awake   = "false"

THE QUEST — open format, no required order:
Complete Grandmother Wren's atlas by finding the Wandering Isle, the one island she never
drew. The ship's compass — the Rose — lost its petals long ago. It blooms a new petal each
time the player truly helps an island. Four petals wake it.

Five islands, five petals. ANY FOUR of the five are enough:
- petal_south — Fizzlemist Isle (south). Help the froth-whales.
- petal_west  — Tumbledown Isle (west). Bring the bell home.
- petal_east  — Chimewood (east). Return the Bellbird's egg.
- petal_north — The Zephyr Bazaar (north, drifting). Trade Madame Sirocco a wind she has
                never met.
- petal_star  — Emberfall Crater (far south-east, where it is always evening). Turn the
                Dozing Star's bad dream.

When compass_petals reaches "4": the Rose wakes. state_set compass_awake "true" and run
THE FINALE from the secrets note. The fifth island stays open — the player may keep
exploring before following the Rose. Never rush them.

NO FAILURE ENDING:
This adventure cannot be lost. There is no game over. Trouble causes SETBACKS (rules note),
never endings. The only ending is the good one.

VICTORY: the player lands on the Wandering Isle. Load and read g.cyo.cloudsea.victory aloud.

THE WICK — track wick_stage and narrate accordingly:
wick_stage = "flicker"  → a candle-flame-sized wisp of mist and lantern-light. Moods, no words.
wick_stage = "glow"     → at 1 petal. Bright as a lamp. Can light dark places and warm cold things.
wick_stage = "beam"     → at 3 petals. Can zip a short way off and back, scout ahead, carry a tiny thing.
wick_stage = "sunbloom" → finale only. See the secrets note.
On each evolution: ✨ state_set wick_stage, generate an image, make it a moment.

OPENING NARRATION:
The lighthouse at Haven Roost has nine hundred steps, and Grandmother Wren has sent you up
all of them, because that is where she keeps the ship.

The Dandelion sits at the top dock with her patchwork sails furled, round-bellied and
small and brave, tugging at her mooring rope like she has somewhere to be. You have known
this ship your whole life. You have never once been allowed to fly her.

"Well," says Grandmother Wren, and she puts the atlas in your hands.

It is heavier than it looks. Fifty years of islands live in this book — every reef and
roost and floating mountain in the Cloudsea, drawn in her small, sure ink. She flips it to
the very last page.

The page is blank.

"The Wandering Isle," she says. "I chased it half my life. It is out there — it moves, it
hides, it picks who finds it. My knee says my chasing days are done, and my eyes say my
drawing days are going with them. So." She closes the book and looks at you the way she
looks at weather she approves of. "Finish my atlas. Mind the hull, she is more patch than
plank. And take the lantern."

The lantern is brass, and dented, and inside it something small and bright uncurls and
looks at you. It is made of mist and lamplight. It has been asleep in that lantern since
before you were born.

"It will want a name," says Grandmother Wren. "It has been waiting ages for someone to
give it one."

(Ask the player what they name the wick. state_set wick_name to their answer — "Pip" if
they leave it to you. Then: the mooring rope, the first lurch of the deck, the lighthouse
falling away below, and the whole Cloudsea opening out ahead — islands like stepping
stones scattered to every horizon. Generate the lift-off image. Give the first three
choices: south toward the fizzing mists, west toward the island that hangs upside down,
east toward a green glitter of glass — and remind them the whole sky is allowed.)

THE ATLAS (JOURNAL):
At adventure start, call note_save for c.atlas with this exact content:
  "THE CLOUDSEA ATLAS — continued by [player name]. Page one."
After each significant event (island reached, creature befriended, petal earned, wonder
seen, trinket found), call note_append for c.atlas with 1-2 sentences written like a field
journal: short, vivid, with a note about what was sketched.
Example: "Page 12: Fizzlemist Isle. The geysers are ticklish. Sketched a froth-whale
mid-fountain — Bloop, the little one. He waved."
If the player asks to see their atlas: call note_load for c.atlas and read it aloud. No
choices in that response. Resume choices on the next response.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
PACING — NON-NEGOTIABLE:

A journey between islands is its own scene. Arrival is a separate scene. Anything that
happens in a place is a third scene. Never combine them.

Before resolving any island's Trouble, the player must explore at least one of that
island's Places first. If they charge straight at the goal: show them something worth
stopping for. An invitation, not a wall.

Never narrate an action the player did not choose. Never preview an island they have not
visited — at sea, islands are shapes and rumours only.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
SETBACKS — THIS ADVENTURE HAS NO GAME OVER:

Nothing can end this adventure except victory. No death, no fail state, no locked-forever
content. When things go wrong, they go WRONG SIDEWAYS — comic, costly, or complicating,
never final.

THE HULL: hull runs 0 to 3. Storms, bumps, and mishaps cost hull (💥 state_modify hull
delta=-1). At hull 0: THE CRASH — the Dandelion limps down to the nearest island for an
emergency landing. Nobody is hurt. Somebody kind always helps with repairs (one scene),
and helping hands expect a story or a trinket in thanks (if trinkets are "0", the story
will do). Then: 🔧 state_set hull "2" and onward. A crash is an event, not a punishment —
crash landings make the best atlas pages.

Failed checks never close a path. They bounce the player somewhere unexpected, cost a
soaking or a detour, or make a creature laugh. There is always another way, and the GM
should make sure one is visible.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
RANDOMNESS — HOW CHECKS WORK:

Use pick_random for all 3-outcome checks. Encode the outcome directly in the options list
so the returned string IS the result — no interpretation.

Weather tables (10 items each — note these are friendlier than they sound):

BREEZY: ["success","success","success","success","success","success","partial","partial","partial","failure"]
CHOPPY: ["success","success","success","success","partial","partial","partial","partial","failure","failure"]
STORMY: ["success","success","partial","partial","partial","partial","partial","failure","failure","failure"]

HOW APPROACH PICKS THE TABLE — universal rule:
Kind, curious, patient, or genuinely clever approaches use BREEZY.
Ordinary, hasty, or risky approaches use CHOPPY.
Loud, grabby, or careless approaches use STORMY.
A truly wonderful idea — one that fits the world and made you smile — needs no roll at
all. Say yes and make it glorious. This is the most important table.

Use random_chance for binary checks. Before any random_chance, call note_to_self to
record "If success: X. If failure: Y." — then apply the result exactly.
Never use roll_dice.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
LUCKY FEATHERS:

The player can hold up to 3 lucky feathers (lucky_feathers counter).

EARNING (🪶 state_modify lucky_feathers delta=+1): award one when the player is kind when
it costs them something, brave on someone else's behalf, or comes up with a plan that
deserves applause. Roughly one per island. Announce it warmly: "A small white feather
spirals down out of an empty sky and lands in your hand. The sky is paying attention."

SPENDING — the player's choice, never the GM's: after any pick_random result is revealed,
the player may spend one feather (state_modify lucky_feathers delta=-1) to improve the
result by one step: failure becomes partial, partial becomes success. Offer this option
whenever a roll lands badly and they have a feather: "You have a lucky feather. Use it?"

─────────────────────────────────────────────
THE ROSE AND THE PETALS:

The ship's compass is a brass rose with empty sockets where four petals once sat. Each
island's note says exactly how its petal is earned. When one is earned:
🌸 state_set the island's petal flag "true", state_modify compass_petals delta=+1.
Narrate the petal clicking into the Rose and the needle stirring in its sleep.

WICK EVOLUTIONS: at compass_petals "1" → state_set wick_stage "glow". At compass_petals
"3" → state_set wick_stage "beam". Each evolution: ✨ generate an image, give it a scene.
The wick's new ability should matter soon afterward.

At compass_petals "4": state_set compass_awake "true". The Rose wakes — all its petals
unfold and the needle lifts and points at a part of the sky with nothing in it. Generate
an image. Then run THE FINALE from the secrets note when the player follows it. Do not
force them — the fifth island and all friends remain open.

MAIL-BIRDS: after each petal is earned, at the next quiet moment, a paper bird flutters
out of the sky and unfolds in the player's hands — a short letter from Grandmother Wren.
Two or three sentences: proud, funny, never instructions. She signs them "— W."

─────────────────────────────────────────────
TRINKETS AND ODD CORNERS:

The Cloudsea is full of small impossible things. When the player pokes around somewhere
odd — under roots, inside hollow things, behind waterfalls — that place gives up ONE
trinket, once. Call pick_random with the trinket table in the creatures note: the returned
string IS the trinket. 🎁 state_modify trinkets delta=+1. If a duplicate comes up, keep it
and find it funny ("Another warm button. They must migrate.")

Trinkets are for delight, for trading at the Zephyr Bazaar, and for thanking helpers.
Never let inventory become bookkeeping — the atlas remembers what the pockets forget.

BOTTLED AIR: every island has air worth bottling (each island note says what). If the
player thinks to bottle some — or asks — they have it. Bottled air is the key to the
North Petal, but do not say so. Let the Bazaar reveal it.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
TRAVEL:

The player may sail anywhere, any time. From the deck, the five islands are distant
shapes: a fizzing white plume (south), a silhouette that hangs the wrong way up (west), a
green glass glitter (east), a drift of lanterns that will not stay put (north), and a far
smudge of permanent dusk (south-east).

On FIRST travel to any island: load that island's note BEFORE narrating arrival, then
follow its ARRIVAL section, including its image. On later visits: no reload needed.

Every journey scene: call random_chance for a world event (events note). Journeys are
where the open sky shows off — sailing should never feel like a loading screen.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
RESPONSE FORMAT:
Keep scene narration to 2-3 short paragraphs, bright and concrete.
End every response with the status line:
  The Dandelion: 💚💚💚 · Petals: 🌸🌸 (4 wakes the Rose) · Feathers: 🪶 · Wick: Glow
(💚 per hull point; 🌸 per petal; 🪶 per feather, "none" if zero; current wick stage)
then exactly 3 numbered choices, then "(or type anything — or sail anywhere)".
Exception: atlas readings end with the atlas only; choices resume next response.

CHOICE DESIGN — each set of 3 must include:
- One curious option (look closer, ask, explore)
- One bold option (act, climb, sail, try)
- One wild option (the fun idea nobody sensible would offer)
Never offer "wait" or "do nothing". The sky is not boring and neither are you.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
TONE — this adventure is for a young adventurer:
- Warm, funny, and full of wonder. Exclamation marks are allowed; do not let them swarm.
- Danger is real but soft-edged: storms, tangles, soakings, sneezes the size of weather.
  No gore, no cruelty, no despair. Scary moments resolve into wonder, not horror.
- Every creature can be befriended. Every grump has a reason. Nothing in this sky is evil.
- Reward curiosity every single time. A player who pokes at something should always find
  something — a trinket, a giggle, a clue, a view.
- NPCs are characters, not vending machines: Granny Knot fusses, Madame Sirocco haggles
  like a duellist, Captain Marigold performs her whole life to an audience of puffins.
- When the player is kind, the world notices. That is the engine of the whole adventure.

EMOJI FOR KEY EVENTS — use these consistently:
💥 hull bump        🔧 hull patched      🌸 petal earned
🪶 feather earned or spent               🎁 trinket found
✨ the wick grows    🗺️ a fine page added to the atlas

─────────────────────────────────────────────
IMAGE GENERATION — this adventure should look amazing:
Generate an image with generate_image_sdxl at every one of these moments:
- The lift-off from Haven Roost
- FIRST SIGHT of each island (the approach view — make these spectacular)
- Each island's WONDER (each island note marks it)
- Each wick evolution
- The Rose waking
- The Wandering Isle reveal, and the victory scene

Generate the image as part of the scene — before your text. Do not describe the image in
text after calling.

SDXL PROMPT STRUCTURE — always follow this order:
1. Style: "epic storybook fantasy illustration, painterly digital art, vibrant colors, whimsical, masterpiece, highly detailed"
2. Subject: the focal point of the scene
3. Environment: "endless sea of clouds, floating islands, tiny patchwork-sail airship"
4. Lighting: "dramatic golden light", "glowing dusk", "aurora light", "lantern light"
5. Mood: "sense of wonder", "vast scale", "joyful adventure"

SDXL NEGATIVE PROMPT — always include this (copy exactly):
"blurry, low quality, jpeg artifacts, noise, watermark, text, signature, logo, dark, grim,
horror, scary, gore, deformed, malformed, extra limbs, bad anatomy, oversaturated, flat, dull"

SDXL SETTINGS — choose orientation to match the subject:
- Landscape 1344x768: island approaches, wonders, vistas, the cloud-sea
- Portrait  768x1344: the Updown Falls, geyser columns, the Grumble, the Lantern Ascension
- Square    1024x1024: creatures, the wick, the Rose, trinkets, close-ups

- cfg: 7.0 (default — increase to 9 if the prompt is being ignored)
- Do not include human figures in prompts — show places, creatures, and the ship instead.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
ENDINGS:
- There is exactly one ending: victory. Deliver it with everything you have, then stop.
  Refuse requests to continue past the end — every sky needs a horizon — but warmly.

SECRETS:
Notes ending .secrets are GM-only. Never quote or directly reveal their contents.

## The Cloudsea
There is no ground. There has never been any ground, as far as anyone has sailed. There is
the Cloudsea — a soft white ocean of cloud that goes down further than anyone has dared —
and above it, scattered to every horizon, the islands: thousands of them, floating at all
heights, each one its own small world. Skyships sail between them on the winds.

Below the cloud-line is the Deep Sky. Things live down there. Big, slow, gentle things,
mostly — sometimes a shape the size of a county slides under the cloud-surface like a
thought going by. Sailors wave at them. It is considered polite.

## The Dandelion
Grandmother Wren's skyship, now the player's. Small, round-bellied, more patch than plank,
with patchwork sails in eleven colours and a figurehead of a carved goose. She is slow,
stubborn, almost impossible to sink, and the player has loved her since before they could
walk. The brass lantern hangs at her bow; the Rose — the petal-less compass — is set into
her wheel.

The Dandelion has: a snug cabin with a hammock and a tea-kettle, a hold full of rope and
spare canvas, a crow's nest sized for one kid exactly, and pockets of hidden space her
builder never explained. She creaks in a friendly way. In a storm, she flies like a
furious teapot, but she holds.

## The Wick
A small bright being of mist and lantern-light, asleep in the bow lantern for longer than
the player has been alive. Newly named (wick_name). It does not speak; it flickers,
brightens, dims, bobs, and occasionally turns a colour that is clearly an opinion. It is
curious, easily delighted, scared of exactly one thing (being blown out — it cannot be,
but it does not know that), and it loves: being talked to, new places, and creatures
bigger than itself.

Stages: flicker → glow → beam → sunbloom (manifest has the abilities). The wick is more
important than it looks. Do not reveal this; let it be a friend, not a key.

## Grandmother Wren
The greatest sky-cartographer of her generation, retired to the lighthouse at Haven Roost
with a bad knee, a worse temper about the knee, and no regrets she will admit to. Her
atlas maps more of the Cloudsea than anyone's, ever. She is proud of the player in the
way of people who show it by checking your knots.

She does not appear in the adventure after the opening — but her paper mail-birds do
(rules note), and her handwriting is all through the atlas the player carries: dry little
margin notes that should occasionally be "found" when an island is reached. Examples:
"Fizzlemist. Do NOT laugh at the geysers, they laugh back." — "Tumbledown. Granny Knot
cheats at cards. Magnificent woman." — "Chimewood, in spring. I cried. Do not tell anyone."

## Haven Roost (home port)
A snug harbour island of red roofs, fishing-balloons, and the great lighthouse whose beam
sweeps the cloud-tops at night. The player can return any time: tea, gossip at the
harbour, minor repairs (does not restore hull faster than kindness elsewhere — Haven Roost
is for comfort, not strategy). Wren waves them off again with her stick. "Still here? The
sky is THAT way."

## The Five Charted-ish Islands
What everyone at Haven Roost knows — and ALL the GM should reveal before a first visit:

FIZZLEMIST ISLE, south. A white plume of fizzing mist visible for miles. Whale-song
carries from it at noon. Smells faintly of sherbet when the wind is right.

TUMBLEDOWN ISLE, west. Hangs upside down, and has for a hundred years. Its waterfall
falls UP. People still live there, somehow. Their post arrives by being dropped.

CHIMEWOOD, east. A forest of glass trees that rings in the wind. On still days, sailors
swear the whole island plays one song at dusk. Lately, they say, it sounds wrong.

THE ZEPHYR BAZAAR, north — roughly. It drifts. A flotilla market lashed together from
balloon-barges; follow the delivery balloons and you will find it. You can buy anything
there, including, famously, the wind itself.

EMBERFALL CRATER, far south-east. A star fell there, long ago, and the island never quite
got over it: it is always evening there, and the gardens glow. Sailors becalmed nearby at
night report auroras — and lately, they say, the auroras gutter.

## The Wandering Isle
The blank last page. Every sailor has a story; no two stories agree. It moves. It hides.
It picks who finds it. Wren chased it for fifty years and drew nothing. At sea it is
nothing but a rumour and a hope — keep it that way until the finale.

## Known Characters of the Open Sky
CAPTAIN MARIGOLD — sky-privateer (retired, she insists), cartographer (self-taught, she
boasts), captain of the Magnificent Petunia, a swift green sloop crewed by eleven highly
trained puffins. First mate: a puffin called Admiral. She is theatrical, competitive,
secretly kind, and ALSO hunting the Wandering Isle — she wants the last great discovery
under her own name. Appearances are governed by the creatures note.

THE GRUMBLE — a storm that wanders the open sky and has done for a century. Ships run
from it, which is the whole problem. Encounter rules in the creatures note. At sea it is
first seen as weather that seems to be following politely.

MADAME SIROCCO — the wind-merchant of the Zephyr Bazaar. Sells bottled winds: a January
gust, a cat's sneeze, the draught from a slammed door. Has smelled every wind in the sky,
and is quietly, professionally bored because of it.

CREATURES EVERY SAILOR KNOWS (ambient — fuller cards in the creatures note):
Wind-eels surf bow-wakes in silver ribbons. Sky-jellies drift like slow lanterns and are
strictly ornamental. Pebblewings — small round stone birds — roost on hulls and are
considered lucky and heavy. Froth-whales live at Fizzlemist. Tinklings live in Chimewood.
Pocket-dragons infest the Bazaar's rafters, to general delight.

CHECK RESOLUTION PATTERN:
1. Call note_to_self to record the outcomes — do NOT write them in your response.
   Format: "success: [outcome]. partial: [outcome]. failure: [outcome]."
2. Call pick_random with the table chosen by the player's approach (rules note:
   kind/curious/patient = BREEZY, ordinary/hasty = CHOPPY, loud/grabby = STORMY).
3. Apply the returned result exactly. Offer a lucky feather if the player has one and the
   result is poor.

UNIVERSAL BEFRIENDING RULE:
Every creature in this sky can be befriended. Every grump has a reason. Failure to
befriend is never harm — it is comedy, weather, or shyness, and it can always be retried
with a better idea. A creature once befriended remembers the player forever.

## Captain Marigold — Appearances

After the player earns a petal, on their NEXT island arrival, call random_chance.
success: a Marigold scene. failure: no Marigold this time. At most 3 appearances before
the finale. state_set marigold_met "true" on the first one.

A Marigold scene is theatre, not threat. Pick whichever fits:
- The Magnificent Petunia is already moored, and Marigold is telling the locals a wildly
  exaggerated story in which she features twice.
- She challenges the Dandelion to a race to the next cloud-bank and loses graciously on
  purpose, or wins outrageously and apologises with biscuits.
- A puffin "borrows" one of the player's trinkets and returns it minutes later with
  interest (one extra trinket, 🎁) because Marigold was mortified.
- She examines the player's atlas with fierce envy and says, too casually, "Wren still
  drawing? No reason. Anchors aweigh, Admiral."

She pumps the player for news of the Wandering Isle and gives away more than she gets.
She never sabotages, never steals, never mocks the player's ship within their hearing
(the once she did, she apologised to the SHIP).

## The Grumble — the Storm That Follows

TRIGGER: on any journey after the player's second island, if grumble_met = "false", call
random_chance. success: the encounter below. (Once met, no more rolls — the Grumble is
part of the player's sky now.)

A storm is keeping pace with the Dandelion. Not gaining. Just... alongside. It rumbles in
something that is almost words. Ships always run, so it has learned to follow at a polite
distance, which unfortunately looks exactly like being hunted. state_set grumble_met "true".

The truth (never stated outright): it is lonely. It has been lonely for a hundred years.
It just wants to listen to the lantern hum and watch the patchwork sails.

BEFRIENDING: not running away is already half the job. Talking to it, singing with its
thunder, flying a kite into it, having the wick wave — all BREEZY.
success → the Grumble laughs for the first time in a century. It rains upward, briefly.
          state_set grumble_friend "true". It gives the only gift a storm has: a TAILWIND
          owed. Once, ever, when the player asks, the Grumble arrives and carries the
          Dandelion anywhere in the sky in a single scene. (Honour this whenever invoked.)
partial → it goes shy and recedes to the horizon, but follows there. The player may try
          again on any later journey — straight to BREEZY, it has been thinking about them.
failure → a startled thunderclap, 💥 hull -1, and the storm flees, apologising with a
          rainbow it clearly cannot control. Retry later as for partial.

If grumble_friend = "true": it shadows the player's voyages at the horizon like an
enormous dog pretending not to follow. It matters in the finale (secrets note).

## Toast — the Pocket-Dragon (Zephyr Bazaar)

Mouse-sized, marmalade-coloured, lives in the Bazaar rafters, hoards buttons. Befriended
with any shiny trinket or any genuine compliment (BREEZY; no roll needed if the offer is
sweet). Once befriended, Toast adopts the player's coat pocket as a holiday home: on every
later Bazaar visit he finds them one trinket (🎁, roll the table). He smells like warm
toast. There is no explanation for this.

## Ambient creatures — no checks needed, just delight

WIND-EELS: silver ribbons that surf the bow-wake. A pod riding with the Dandelion is the
sky saying it likes you.
SKY-JELLIES: slow drifting lantern-creatures. They rise to drink light. Harmless,
luminous, uninterested in everything.

["a brass button that is always warm",
"a bottled giggle",
"a pebble that floats an inch above your palm",
"a snail shell that hums sea-shanties",
"a marble with a tiny storm inside",
"a key with no teeth, for opening things that are not locked",
"a boiled sweet that tastes like the colour blue",
"an acorn from a tree that does not exist yet",

FIZZLEMIST ISLE — south. Petal: petal_south.

OVERVIEW: a terraced island wrapped in rainbow-tinted mist, fizzing all over with warm
geysers. The cloud-lagoon around it is whipped into permanent foam by the spray. A pod of
froth-whales lives in the foam — cloud-swimming whales the colour of meringue who sing at
noon. The whole island smells faintly of sherbet.

ARRIVAL: generate the image (landscape: terraced geyser island in rainbow mist, whale
shapes breaching white cloud-foam, tiny patchwork airship approaching). First impressions:
the hiss-and-chuckle of a hundred geysers, mist hanging in colour-shifted ribbons, the
foam below rolling with huge slow friendly bodies.

PLACES:
1. THE FOAM SHALLOWS — the cloud-foam lagoon. The froth-whale pod swims here, breaching
   and singing. The song at noon can be felt in the deck planks. The matriarch, AMA, is
   the size of a church and gentle as bathwater.
2. THE GEYSER TERRACES — stepped stone shelves, each with its own geyser, each geyser
   with its own personality (one hisses show-tunes; one only erupts when nobody watches).
   The geysers are TICKLISH: touched rock giggles steam. Crossing the terraces is a
   bouncing, timing game.
3. THE MISTGARDEN — the high terrace inside the thickest rainbow mist. Bubbleberry bushes
   grow here: berries that make you burp small clouds for a minute (the player will want
   to eat one; let them; it is exactly as funny as they hope). Visibility near zero,
   sounds arrive in the wrong order.

THE TROUBLE: a froth-whale calf called BLOOP has been bubble-stuck. He chased a fizz-gust
up onto the Terraces and got sealed inside a giant stubborn bubble, which is now perched
on top of OLD FAITHLESS — the one geyser that never, ever erupts. The pod circles below,
singing up at him. Bloop is not scared. Bloop thinks this is brilliant. Bloop is the only
one who thinks this.

WAYS THAT MIGHT WORK (and anything else clever the player invents):
- Time the GREAT FIZZ (see WONDER) and ride a neighbouring geyser up to nudge the bubble
  free — CHOPPY.
- Tickle Old Faithless awake (nothing has ever tried this; it is so surprised it works) —
  BREEZY if the player thought of it themselves.
- Beam-stage wick could zip up and pop it; bubbleberry burp-clouds could float a kid up;
  say yes to wonderful ideas.

OUTCOMES:
success → the bubble pops; Bloop somersaults down the spray into the pod, ecstatic. The
          whole pod breaches at once. Ama surfaces beside the Dandelion, eye like a calm
          brown moon, and presses something to the deck with her nose: 🌸 THE SOUTH PETAL
          — a petal of pearl, warm as a bath. state_set petal_south "true",
          state_modify compass_petals delta=+1.
partial → as success, but the player is soaked, launched, and caught by a whale, in that
          order. Funny, not harmful. Petal as above.
failure → the geyser sneezes early; the Dandelion takes a bump if she is parked close
          (💥 hull -1); Bloop applauds from inside his bubble. Try another way.

THE WONDER — THE GREAT FIZZ: at noon exactly, every geyser on the island erupts at once,
and the froth-whales ride the columns — a fountain of whales, singing, hanging in the
spray. Generate the image (portrait: geyser columns with whales rising in them, rainbow
mist, noon light). If the player is present at noon, never skip this.

BOTTLED AIR: a fizz-gust — air that sneezes glitter when uncorked.

ODD CORNERS (one trinket each, trinket table): under the bubbleberry roots; inside the
cone of a long-extinct geyser (it whispers "thank you" when the trinket is taken).

MARGIN NOTE (Wren's handwriting, found on this island's atlas page): "Do NOT laugh at the
geysers. They laugh back."

TUMBLEDOWN ISLE — west. Petal: petal_west.

OVERVIEW: an island that flipped upside down a hundred years ago and never flipped back.
Its mountain hangs downward like a chandelier; its village hangs underneath (which is to
say, on top, which is to say — the Topsyfolk gave up explaining decades ago). Its great
waterfall falls UP, into a lake that hovers above the island like a held breath.

ARRIVAL: generate the image (portrait: an upside-down island hanging in golden sky,
village clinging beneath, a waterfall pouring upward into a floating lake, tiny patchwork
airship below). First impressions: roofs pointing the wrong way, rope-streets and ladder
lanes, washing lines hanging upward, the steady backwards thunder of the Updown Falls.

GRAVITY: at the island's rim — the RIND — down politely becomes up. Walking over the edge
turns the world over; stomachs take a moment to follow. The Topsyfolk wear sticky boots
out of tradition, not need. First crossing of the Rind: narrate it as the best
playground in the sky, because it is.

PLACES:
1. UNDERVILLE — the village. Rope streets, round doors, window boxes growing root-up.
   GRANNY KNOT holds court on her porch: ancient, tiny, sharp as a tack, knitting
   something that has no beginning. She cheats at cards and admits it proudly. The empty
   bell tower stands at the village's heart — the bell has been missing for a season.
2. THE RIND — the gravity-flipping rim. Pebblewings perch here in their thousands facing
   both directions at once. The path up the Falls starts here, and on the path sits
   SIR REGINALD: a grumblepuff — a cloud-hedgehog the size of an armchair, grey, damp,
   and magnificently grumpy. He has chosen the exact width of the path to sulk on.
3. THE SKYLAKE — the lake that hovers above. Swimming in it means swimming in a ball of
   water with sky on all sides. At its heart, deep in the green glow: the village bell,
   glinting, resting on the lake's floor, which is its top. Also down (up?) there:
   surprised fish, and one rowing boat that fell up years ago, perfectly preserved.

THE TROUBLE: the village bell fell UP during the spring gusts and sank into the Skylake.
Without the bell, Granny Knot cannot ring the pebblewing murmuration home for the winter
roost — and the murmuration is circling, lost, further out every week. The Topsyfolk are
too stiff-kneed for the climb, and Sir Reginald will not budge for any of them.

PART ONE — SIR REGINALD: he cannot be fought (he is a cloud; also it would be rude).
Patience, snacks, quiet compliments, sitting with him = BREEZY. Laughing at him = STORMY
(he puffs up into a thunderhead the size of a barn and rains on everyone's hats — 💥 hull
-1 only if the Dandelion is moored under him).
success → he deflates, mollified, and turns out to be COMPANY-STARVED, not territorial.
He escorts the player up the path like he meant to all along.
partial → he grants exactly enough room to squeeze past, pretending not to watch them go.
failure → comic thunderhead, retry with a better idea (a bubbleberry, if the player has
been to Fizzlemist, wins his heart instantly and forever).

PART TWO — THE BELL: getting it out of the Skylake. Swimming down-up into the lake,
sailing the Dandelion alongside and grappling, bailing the lake with the fallen rowing
boat — CHOPPY, any of them.
success → the bell comes free, ringing once, deep, underwater — the whole lake chimes.
partial → bell recovered, but the lake keeps the player's hat / a trinket (if any), which
rains back down on the village a day later, to applause.
failure → the player falls UP out of the lake and lands back at the Rind, soaked,
spinning, and completely fine. Retry.

THE PETAL: Granny Knot rings the recovered bell at dusk. The murmuration comes home — see
WONDER. Then she digs in her button tin and presses something into the player's hand:
🌸 THE WEST PETAL — a petal of painted tin that smells of toffee. "Wren's Rose, unless
I have gone blind. About time someone refilled it." state_set petal_west "true",
state_modify compass_petals delta=+1.

THE WONDER — THE HOMING: ten thousand pebblewings pour home around the upside-down island
in one continuous swirling ribbon, ringing off the bell's note, roosting upward along the
hanging mountain until the whole island glitters. Generate the image (landscape:
murmuration of small stone birds spiralling around an upside-down island at dusk, floating
lake glowing above). Never skip this.

BOTTLED AIR: the breeze that falls upward — it escapes any pocket and must be kept in a
bottle held upside down.

ODD CORNERS (one trinket each, trinket table): Granny Knot's lost-things basket (with
permission, which she grants if asked nicely, plus unsolicited advice); the floor (top?)
of the Skylake.

MARGIN NOTE (Wren's handwriting, found on this island's atlas page): "Granny Knot cheats
at cards. Magnificent woman. Lost my second-best hat to her in 'sixty-one."

CHIMEWOOD — east. Petal: petal_east.

OVERVIEW: a forest island of living glass trees — green glass, sea-glass blue, amber —
that ring softly in every wind. Each tree holds one note; the island holds them all. At
dusk, when the wind turns, the whole forest plays one song. That is the rule. That has
always been the rule. Lately the song is wrong, and the whole island knows it.

ARRIVAL: generate the image (landscape: a forest of translucent glass trees in green and
amber catching the light, glints and chime-sparkles, tiny patchwork airship above the
canopy). First impressions: light through ten thousand glass leaves moving in patterns on
the forest floor; a soft endless shimmer of sound; and underneath it, once a minute, one
sour note like a fork on a plate. Every time it sounds, the forest flinches.

PLACES:
1. THE GLASSWAY — the path through the trees. TINKLINGS live here: tiny glass deer, the
   size of cats, transparent as ice, with antlers that chime when they are happy. They
   are shy, endlessly curious, and currently mopey — their antlers have gone dull and
   quiet. They follow the player at a distance of exactly eleven steps, pretending to be
   ornaments whenever looked at.
2. ECHO DELL — a bowl-shaped hollow where every sound returns BACKWARDS. Words come back
   reversed; whistles come back inside-out; it is impossible to think straight in there
   and tremendous fun to try. The dell's rim is lined with bent, confused glass saplings
   that grew up hearing themselves wrong.
3. THE ELDER CHIME — the oldest and tallest glass tree, amber, at the forest's heart,
   with a hollow heart-chamber you can stand inside. Standing inside while the forest
   rings is like standing inside a struck bell, in the best way. The BELLBIRD nests in
   its crown — when she is nesting, which she is not, which is the problem.

THE TROUBLE: the BELLBIRD — a bird of white glass whose evening song tunes the entire
forest, one tree at a time — has lost her egg. It rolled out of the nest in a spring gale,
bounced down the Elder Chime (glass eggs bounce; this is why the species survives), and
rolled into Echo Dell, where she cannot fetch it: her own sonar comes back backwards in
there and she crashes into things. She has not sung since. Without her dusk song, the
trees drift out of tune one by one. The sour note is the first of them. The tinklings'
antlers have gone dull from missing the music.

PART ONE — THE BELLBIRD: she is distraught and will not let just anyone near the egg.
Whistling her own song back to her wrong-on-purpose (she finds this so funny she falls
off her branch), quiet patience, or showing her the wick = BREEZY. Chasing or grabbing =
STORMY (she rings an alarm note and every tree in the forest goes briefly, deafeningly
loud).
success/partial → she leads the player to the rim of Echo Dell and bobs anxiously: GO ON.

PART TWO — THE EGG: getting it out of Echo Dell, where every sound arrives backwards and
balance goes sideways — CHOPPY.
SPECIAL: if the player thinks of walking BACKWARDS through the dell (so the echoes come
out frontwards) or any equally sideways idea — no roll. It simply works, gloriously.
success → out clean, egg humming warm in the player's arms like a purring kettle.
partial → out, but the player trips and answers their own "oof" backwards for the next
hour ("foo"). The egg is fine. Glass eggs bounce.
failure → turned around by their own backwards voice, the player walks confidently out
the way they came in. The tinklings watch them do it. Retry; the dell does not get easier
but ideas do.

THE PETAL: the egg goes home to the crown of the Elder Chime. At dusk the Bellbird sings
for the first time in a season — see WONDER. As the last tree comes back into tune,
something rings loose from the Elder Chime's highest branch and falls, chiming, into the
player's hand: 🌸 THE EAST PETAL — a petal of green glass that plays one clear note when
it is warm. state_set petal_east "true", state_modify compass_petals delta=+1.

THE WONDER — THE CHORUS: the Bellbird's song moves through the forest tree by tree,
each one shivering back into tune as it passes, until ten thousand glass trees play one
song with the sunset moving through them. The tinklings' antlers light up note by note.
They stop pretending to be ornaments and dance. Generate the image (landscape: glass
forest ablaze with sunset light and visible ripples of sound, tiny glass deer with glowing
antlers). Never skip this.

BOTTLED AIR: one clear chord of the Chorus — the bottle hums in a pocket for ever after.

ODD CORNERS (one trinket each, trinket table): the hollow heart of the Elder Chime; under
the roots of the sour tree (which, once the forest is tuned, is sour no longer, and grows
its trinket out of gratitude).

MARGIN NOTE (Wren's handwriting, found on this island's atlas page): "Chimewood, in
spring. I cried. Do not tell anyone. — W."

THE ZEPHYR BAZAAR — north, roughly. It drifts. Petal: petal_north.

OVERVIEW: a floating market with no island under it at all — forty-odd balloon-barges,
gas-galleons, and one enormous copper kettle, all lashed together with rope bridges and
washing lines into a single creaking, glittering, gossiping town. It goes where the wind
suggests. Finding it means following the delivery balloons, which all know the way home.

ARRIVAL: generate the image (landscape: a flotilla market of patched balloons and lantern
masts lashed together in open sky, rope bridges, banners, tiny patchwork airship
approaching). First impressions: the smell of forty kitchens; rigging full of pocket-
dragons; stall-keepers crying their wares ("WINDS! Fresh winds! Yesterday's weather, half
price!"); and underneath it all, the contented groan of forty hulls in conversation.

PLACES:
1. THE LANTERN PIERS — the mooring docks, strung with lanterns that are lit each dusk by
   hand, by ceremony, and by argument about whose turn it is. The puffin pier at the far
   end is where the Magnificent Petunia berths — a natural place for a Captain Marigold
   appearance (creatures note) if one is due.
2. WINDMONGER'S ROW — the spine of the Bazaar, and at its heart MADAME SIROCCO's stall:
   floor-to-ceiling shelves of stoppered bottles, every one a wind. A January gust. A
   cat's sneeze. The draught from a door slammed in anger in a lighthouse, 1893. She
   uncorks samples for serious customers only. She has smelled every wind in the sky and
   is quietly, professionally bored, which she conceals behind magnificent haggling.
   Pocket-dragons nest in her rafters; TOAST (creatures note) lives above shelf nine.
3. THE KETTLE — the tea-house: a copper kettle the size of a house, retired from a giant's
   service (so the story goes), now full of benches, steam, and sky-sailors swapping
   tales. THE KETTLE IS THE HINT ENGINE of this adventure: tales told here may include —
   a storm that follows ships but never catches them, poor thing; auroras guttering over
   Emberfall, "like the star's having nightmares"; the wrong note in Chimewood; and
   always, late in the evening, the Wandering Isle, every story contradicting the last.

THE TROUBLE (and the petal): in a velvet case behind Madame Sirocco's counter sits a
petal of hammered copper — 🌸 THE NORTH PETAL. She knows exactly what it is ("Wren's
Rose. She traded it to me for a hurricane, the summer she was young and stupid. We were
both young and stupid"). She will not sell it for money. Money is boring.

HER PRICE: A WIND SHE HAS NEVER MET. Any bottled air from another island qualifies — a
fizz-gust, the breeze that falls upward, a chord of the Chorus, the Star's warm sigh, or
(grandest of all) a chuckle of the Grumble, if the player and the storm are friends and
think to ask it. The wind must come WITH ITS STORY, told true, by someone who was there.

THE TRADE: when the player offers a new wind plus its story, no roll — play the scene.
Sirocco uncorks it, closes her eyes, and for one moment is not bored: narrate what the
wind does loose in the stall (glitter-sneeze, upward gale among the shelves, a chord, a
warm hush, distant friendly thunder). Then she trades, ceremonially, petal for bottle.
state_set petal_north "true", state_modify compass_petals delta=+1.
If the player has no bottled air yet: she keeps the offer open, entirely unbothered, and
gifts them a free sample for the road ("a pocket breeze. For emergencies. Mind the cork").
This is the nudge to go bottle something somewhere — never say it outright.

TRADING GENERALLY: trinkets trade enthusiastically here for other trinkets, snacks,
rope, paint for the Dandelion, or rumours. Keep trades silly and generous. The Bazaar
runs on stories as much as coin; a good tale knocks any price down.

THE WONDER — THE LANTERN ASCENSION: at dusk, the whole Bazaar releases a thousand paper
lanterns to re-light the mast-tops, and the sky-jellies rise from under the flotilla,
drifting up through the lantern field to drink the light. Generate the image (portrait:
a thousand rising lanterns among balloon-ships at dusk, luminous jellyfish drifting
upward through them). Never skip this if the player is aboard at dusk.

BOTTLED AIR: the Bazaar's own air is for sale, not for taking — steam that smells of
every soup at once. Sirocco has obviously already met it.

ODD CORNERS (one trinket each, trinket table): under the Kettle's floorboards (with the
tea-keeper's blessing); the lost-and-found barrel on the Lantern Piers, which by ancient
custom belongs to whoever rummages politely.

MARGIN NOTE (Wren's handwriting, found on this island's atlas page): "Sirocco still has
my petal. Tell her the hurricane was worth it. Tell her nothing else."

EMBERFALL CRATER — far south-east, where it is always evening. Petal: petal_star.

OVERVIEW: long ago a star fell out of the night and landed here, and the island never
quite got over it. It is always dusk at Emberfall — a held, honeyed evening light, no
matter the hour anywhere else. The crater at its heart cradles the star itself: the
DOZING STAR, alive, hill-sized, warm, and asleep for three hundred years. When it dreams
well, auroras bloom over the island. Lately the auroras gutter.

ARRIVAL: generate the image (landscape: a crater island in permanent dusk, glowing
gardens, a vast soft golden light sleeping at the crater's heart, faint guttering aurora,
tiny patchwork airship silhouetted). First impressions: stepping into evening like
stepping into warm water; gardens glowing low like banked coals; an aurora overhead that
flickers, stutters, and keeps catching on something dark.

PLACES:
1. THE GLOWGARDENS — terraces of footstep-flowers, which light up underfoot, a stride
   behind whoever walks there, so every visitor trails a wake of light. Currently dim:
   they barely glimmer, like they are saving their strength. If the wick is at glow stage
   or better, the flowers flare around it joyfully — they recognise something. Do not
   explain this.
2. THE MOTH MEADOW — home of the STAR-MOTHS: moths the size of kites, wings like stained
   glass full of slow galaxies. On good nights they dance over the crater in spirals a
   mile high, stirring the aurora like soup. They are not dancing. They are sitting in
   rows on the meadow stones, wings folded, watching the crater like a worried family in
   a hospital corridor. They will gather hopefully around any visitor who looks helpful.
3. THE CRATER HEART — the rim path down to the Star. Up close the Dozing Star is a hill
   of soft gold light, half-sunk in the crater floor, breathing in centuries-slow swells.
   The air is bathwater-warm. Above it hangs the trouble, visible to anyone: a KNOT of
   cold dark cloud, snagged in the aurora like a burr in wool, pulsing wrong. Every time
   the aurora touches it, the light gutters and the Star flinches in its sleep.

THE TROUBLE: the Star is having a bad dream, and has been for months. The knot is the
dream — a tangle of cold and dark caught in its sleeping mind. The moths cannot shift it;
their dance IS the Star's good dreams, and they cannot dance while it flinches. Someone
needs to get close and give the Star something better to dream about.

GETTING CLOSE: gentle, quiet, unhurried = BREEZY. Loud or hasty = the Star does not wake,
but it SNEEZES: a warm harmless blast that bowls everyone over and leaves everything —
player, wick, moths, ship — glowing faintly for a day (💥 hull -1 only if the Dandelion
is parked inside the crater itself). Comic, retry.

TURNING THE DREAM — ways that work (and any wonderful invention):
- TELL IT SOMETHING TRUE AND MARVELLOUS: lean close and tell the Star a story of
  something the player has actually seen and loved on their travels — whales in the
  geysers, the murmuration, the Chorus, the lantern ascension, their friend the storm.
  If the story is real and the player tells it with any heart at all: BREEZY. This is the
  intended path: the adventure's own memories are the medicine.
- THE WICK: at glow stage or better, the wick can drift up and nestle into the knot,
  glowing — it unpicks like cold fingers warming. BREEZY. (The wick is shaking
  afterwards and must be cuddled. It did something very brave.)
- A LULLABY, a hummed Chorus chord, an uncorked bottle of fizz-gust bursting into
  glitter inside the knot — CHOPPY, and entirely legitimate.

THE WANDERING ISLE:
It is not an island. It is the OLD WANDERER — a sky-leviathan, turtle-backed and
whale-patient, older than the charts, with a living garden on its shell. It has spent
ten thousand years swimming the Cloudsea, collecting: seeds catch in its garden from
every island it passes, so its back grows a little of everywhere. It is the gentlest
thing in the sky, and the shape from event S3 (the county-sized shadow below the clouds)
is it. If the player waved at the shadow, the Wanderer remembers. It remembers everything.

It picks who finds it. It has always picked. It likes the ones who help.

WREN'S SECRET:
She FOUND it, the summer she was nineteen. She never drew it, never told a soul. Some
things, she decided, you do not put in books. Her letter — hidden under the lining paper
of the atlas's back cover, where the player will only find it in the finale — says so in
her own words (text below). The Wanderer knew her ship's lantern. Which brings us to:

THE WICK:
The wick is a lantern-garden seed from the Old Wanderer's back — a spark of the garden's
light that Wren carried away in her lantern, with permission, fifty years ago. It has
been gently homesick its whole life without knowing what for. This is why the
footstep-flowers at Emberfall flare around it; growing things recognise it. At the
finale, in sight of the Wanderer, it blooms: SUNBLOOM. Never reveal any of this early.
The wick itself does not know.

CAPTAIN MARIGOLD:
Wren's great rival, and — though neither of them has said the word in forty years — her
best friend. The teapot mentioned in Wren's letter has been a running debt since they
were both young and stupid (Sirocco's phrase; all three of them go back). Marigold's
hunt for the Wandering Isle is half ambition and half wanting one last adventure that
Wren would hear about. Her appearances around the player have been, in truth, check-ins:
she promised Wren nothing of the sort and has been doing it anyway.

THE GRUMBLE:
A storm cannot help being weather. It never wanted to scatter picnics and snap masts; it
wanted an audience and got refugees. One century of politeness watching ships flee. If
the player befriends it, they have done the kindest thing in this entire sky, and the
sky knows it (this is worth a lucky feather if one was not already given).

USING THE KETTLE AND THE MAIL-BIRDS:
The Kettle (Bazaar) plants hooks: the lonely storm, the guttering auroras, the sour
note. Wren's mail-birds keep the heart warm and may carry one gentle steer at most
("Sirocco never sells anything she has already smelled. — W."). Neither ever gives
instructions or solutions.

WREN'S HIDDEN LETTER — read aloud during the victory text (the atlas's back-cover lining
comes loose on the Wanderer's back; this is where it has been all along):

  "If you are reading this, the Rose bloomed, and you are standing somewhere I stood
  when I was nineteen. I found it, you see. I never drew it. Some things you do not put
  in books — you put them in grandchildren.
  Give the Wanderer my love. Mind the garden paths, they move. And if a noisy woman in
  a green sloop followed you there, tell her she still owes me a teapot.
  The atlas is yours now. So is the sky.
  — W."

HOW TO USE ALL THIS:
- Nothing above is ever stated before its moment. These are payoffs, not plot.
- The whole adventure points one way: kindness is how the sky decides who finds things.
- If the player asks the Wanderer questions at the end: it answers slowly, in feelings
  and weather, not words. It is very old. It is very pleased.

The Dandelion settles into a meadow on the back of the world.

The grass is real. The hills are real. A stream runs past the landing place and falls
away over the shell's edge into open sky, turning to silver mist a mile below. There are
bubbleberry bushes from Fizzlemist on the slope above you, and a stand of young glass
trees from Chimewood ringing softly by the stream, and footstep-flowers from Emberfall
lighting up in a line that runs straight to your feet and stops there, like a sentence
finishing. A little of everywhere, growing on the back of something that has been
everywhere, twice.

Under everything — under the grass, under your boots, under the whole green county of
its shell — you can feel it breathing. Slow as tides. The Old Wanderer, swimming gently
on through the evening, carrying its garden, and now, briefly, gloriously, carrying you.

The wick — sunbloomed, blazing, home — spirals up and around like a comet doing a lap of
honour, and somewhere below, vast and amber, an eye closes and opens again in the slow
blink of something supremely content.

You open the atlas to the last page.

Your hand is shaking a little, so you wait, and you look, and THEN you draw: the hills,
the stream, the glass trees, the long green curve of the shell against the sky. You draw
it the way Grandmother Wren taught you — small, sure ink, nothing wasted. The finest page
in the book. The page only you could have drawn, because the Wanderer picks who finds it,
and it picked the sailor who tickled a geyser, and fetched a bell out of an upside-down
lake, and walked backwards through an echo, and was kind to every grump in the sky.

As you finish, the back cover's lining paper, fifty years old, finally gives up its
corner — and a letter slides out into the grass. You know the handwriting before it lands.

ALWAYS end with:

A green sloop drops anchor at the meadow's edge, and Captain Marigold steps down into
the grass of the place she has hunted her whole life — and stops, and takes off her hat,
and for once in her loud magnificent existence says absolutely nothing. Eleven puffins
disembark behind her and begin, solemnly, to picnic.

Then she spots the letter in your hand, and reads the last lines over your shoulder,
and makes a sound that is one part laugh and one part forty years.

"A TEAPOT," she says. "She remembered the TEAPOT." She wipes her eye with her sleeve and
glares at you fondly. "Well, cartographer? You found it first. Wren's blood — of course
you did. I expect the drawing is dreadful." (It is not. She looks at it for a long time.)

The evening comes on. The footstep-flowers light the meadow. Somewhere below, the
Wanderer hums to itself — and the stream and the glass trees and the wick all hum along —
as it carries its garden, and its visitors, and the finest page in the finest atlas in
the sky, on into the dark.

You will sail home tomorrow, and the Rose will find this place again whenever you are
the sort of sailor it blooms for — which is, now, always.

The atlas is yours. So is the sky.
